title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Q&A session at the SumZero Top Stocks Investor Summit on February 9, 2023
summary: Days after the Turkish earthquake, Pabrai explains how he weighs country risk against business quality using Munger's Belridge Oil story, and walks through his Turkish holdings (Reysas, TAV Airports, the Coke bottler), Brookfield, Prosus/Tencent, Indian Energy Exchange, Adani, Amazon, Apple and Microsoft. Key takeaways: hang on for dear life to the rare great business (his Ferrari sale was a big mistake), unhedged lira exposure is fine if assets are inflation-indexed, and he avoids macro calls and the 'law of large numbers' mega-caps.

ideas.idea: Munger's Belridge Oil mistake shows that overrating a manager's flaw and underrating a business's basic economics is how great investments get passed up.
ideas.detail: In 1977 Munger bought 300 shares at $115 (~$35,000) at 10-15% of liquidation value, then declined 1,200 more because the CEO was an alcoholic; Shell bought Belridge in 1979 for $3.6 billion (30x) and the proceeds went into Berkshire at ~$300/share, now ~$500,000, roughly 45,000x. 'The oilfield didn't drink.'

ideas.idea: Country risk deserves some weight but rejecting a business simply because it is in Turkey is wrong; investments always come with some hair on them.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Macro issues like high inflation and irrational monetary policy exist, but the more rationally you weigh the factors the better the decision. Meta likewise had great and not-so-great aspects to weigh.

ideas.idea: The Turkish Coke bottler (Coca-Cola Icecek) has the same economics as any bottler worldwide yet trades at barely double-digit multiples, having been at 4-5x cash flow a year earlier.
ideas.detail: Exclusive rights in Turkey plus 12 other countries including 49% of the Pakistan bottler (Coke owns 51% and will likely sell); Coca-Cola owns 20% and sits on the board and even subsidized their purchase of a Central Asian bottler. The promoter family also runs a 50%-share beer business and a dominant supermarket, the highest-quality management team he met in Turkey.

ideas.idea: Reysas was too small to become the 10% position he wanted, so he bought a third of the company for $7-8 million when the market cap was $16 million.
ideas.detail: The fund managed ~$700 million; after the earthquake the market cap is $250-300 million against liquidation value now north of $1.5 billion, so it has moved from 2% to 20-25% of liquidation value. The lira went from 5 to ~19 per dollar (a 75% loss) yet the stock is up ~16x in dollars over 3.5 years.

ideas.idea: What attracted him to Reysas was not liquidation value but reinvestment: the father-son team demand payback in dollars within 2-3 years, implying 25-35% IRRs.
ideas.detail: They enter new businesses by starting small to gain competence, then scale; he plans to let it ride 20 years and hopes to 'go to my grave with it', imagining $10-30 billion by 2040-2043. He has no desire to sit on the board; they can run circles around him and he hasn't seen them do anything dumb in 15 years.

ideas.idea: He will not lighten up even if two Turkish stocks reach 80% of his offshore fund; investors who dislike it can get off the bus.
ideas.detail: Reysas and TAV Airports collectively make up about half the closed offshore fund through appreciation. He cites the Waltons, who keep 90%+ of their wealth in Walmart without controlling it and are perfectly comfortable.

ideas.idea: Think of yourself as a minority owner of a great business and don't sell when it is fully priced or even overpriced, only when egregiously overpriced.
ideas.detail: If Walmart went to 100x normalized earnings the family might sell, but at 20x, 30x or 40x do nothing. Fewer than 3-5% of listed companies qualify as great businesses; if you own a fraction of one, hang on for dear life.

ideas.idea: Selling Ferrari because it looked optically expensive was one of the dumbest things he did; he would have three times the money had he held.
ideas.detail: Via Fiat Chrysler (bought in 2012 at $5 billion market cap on $140 billion sales, under 4% of revenue) Pabrai Funds owned north of 1% of Ferrari. Ferrari has 80% margins and demand rises with price: the $421,000 Purosangue sold out and trades for ~$1 million. 'Old too soon and wise too late.'

ideas.idea: There is no need to hedge the lira if you own Turkish businesses whose assets and revenues are automatically inflation-indexed.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Warehouses are steel, concrete and land that move with inflation and Reysas's rents are inflation-indexed or in dollars/euros; the Coke bottler can raise prices in lockstep with inflation. Those are the only kinds of Turkish investments he wants.

ideas.idea: Retail US investors can access Turkey only via Fidelity's international desk by phone, at $80-90 per trade plus FX fees; he uses UBS as prime broker.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Frictional costs exist but are acceptable. The Turkish market was closed until February 14 after hitting 10% lower circuits, so prices should be more attractive on reopening.

ideas.idea: Airports are monopoly cash cows if you don't overpay for the concession, and TAV bought Almaty airport outright at ~3x cash flow during the pandemic.
ideas.detail: TAV runs 15 airports in eight countries under BOT concessions mixing regulated passenger fees with unregulated duty free and F&B. Almaty is the only major airport he knows that is privately owned in perpetuity; $400 million plus $250 million capex for an asset that should cash-flow over $200 million a year by 2026, growing 5-7% forever, in landlocked, high-income Kazakhstan. Such assets should trade at 30-40x cash flow.

ideas.idea: The biggest risk in airports is animal spirits, when bidders overpay for new concessions; privately run airports are far better run than government ones.
ideas.detail: Only 4-5% of the world's airports are privately run; LaGuardia today versus five years ago is incomparable and would not have happened under government ownership.

ideas.idea: Brookfield is a high-quality recurring-revenue toll bridge for sovereign wealth funds, with better DNA than private-equity-rooted peers.
ideas.detail: Bruce Flatt sold off mediocre businesses like mining two decades ago to focus on the highest-quality long-lived infrastructure (trophy real estate, hydro, railroads, an Intel foundry deal, music rights), while KKR and Blackstone historically bought mediocre businesses and financially engineered them. Management publishes five-year targets it has been exceeding; a basket of Brookfield, Blackstone, KKR and Apollo would also do well. Upside is far less than in Turkey.

ideas.idea: Work-from-home hurts peripheral office buildings with vacancy, while Brookfield's trophy properties see lower rents rather than vacancy and are protected by long leases.
ideas.detail: Meta signed a long lease on Austin's tallest tower and is already subleasing it, but the landlord still collects rent; Brookfield Place and Canary Wharf are the last to be affected.

ideas.idea: The whole world is heavily picked over; Turkey is uniquely mispriced, and Korea's 0.7-0.8 birth rate is an alarming headwind despite being always cheap.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Japan is at 1.4 and opening to immigration; China also faces decline. The US is the only developed nation with population growth, which is a huge long-run advantage he wishes Congress would protect by fixing immigration.

ideas.idea: He switched his Alibaba loss into Prosus/Tencent because of a big difference in business quality, leadership, and government relations.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Handicapping what the CCP does with Alibaba falls in the 'too hard' pile; Tencent has always been cooperative with the government, while Alibaba's relationship is still not as good. Tencent was his exception to the mega-cap rule.

ideas.idea: Indian Energy Exchange is one of the highest-quality businesses he has seen anywhere, and he paid up 30-40x earnings for the maximum 4.99% foreign stake before the pandemic.
ideas.detail: About 8% of India's power flows through IEX, fees are ~1% of that value and 70-80% drops to the bottom line; with Indian power demand growing 8-9% a year the share could reach 15-30%. The two-year-old Indian Gas Exchange already handles 5% of India's gas in some months at two-thirds pre-tax margins and must be diluted to 25% via IPO, which could rival the parent's market cap. He now owns 1-1.5% and is considering adding.

ideas.idea: He needs no opinion on the Adani controversy; Indian investors he knows never owned it because it was always optically very expensive.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Adani's assets (private airports, ports, pipelines, transmission) are exceptional, and even the Hindenburg report leads with valuation. 'I only need to have an opinion on the stuff we are going to invest in; we'll buy some popcorn and watch the movie.'

ideas.idea: Amazon is the most exceptional business ever created, but he has always been too dumb to buy it and probably always will be.
ideas.detail: He views it as a consumer commerce business with a massive enterprise web infrastructure footprint, whose spawning engine is alive; retail numbers aren't great but fulfillment, advertising and AWS are; Jassy is de-emphasizing low-return businesses and starting buybacks.

ideas.idea: The law of large numbers is a mental block that keeps him out of $1-2 trillion market caps, because the death rate of giant businesses over 50-100 years is very high.
ideas.detail: He can see nothing hurting Apple for 10 years but cannot make that call for 20-40 years, which buying at $2 trillion requires. Ferrari and Hermes will still be cranking in 20-80 years; LVMH has a much stronger chance of existing in 50 years than Amazon. Berkshire's railroad is an indestructible moat over 100-200 years, and Munger corrected him that its power business is pretty good too.

ideas.idea: He would be more interested in Microsoft than Apple because the iPhone is a kludgy device that a future interface shift could displace, and Apple's 30% App Store take rate is not win-win.
ideas.detail: Apple has enormous consumer trust and brand but animosity from developers; Amazon's enterprise customers hold no such negative view. Apple should do well for 10 years, but he wouldn't bet on 20.

ideas.idea: Macro and recession calls are not his strong suit, so he makes bets where such events have little impact.
ideas.detail: He saw the 2000 bubble and sidestepped it but never saw 2008 coming and took the full brunt. The US has a great independent central bank, inflation is benign given the money pumped in, and unemployment is unbelievably low. IEX, Reysas, TAV and the Coke bottler are interesting precisely because he doesn't have to think about macro.

ideas.idea: Donations planned for Dakshana this year should be redirected to Turkish earthquake relief.
ideas.detail: Friends in Turkey suggested the toll could reach 100,000; SumZero has been generous to Dakshana and he asked them and viewers to send that support to Turkey instead, saying he would redirect it anyway.
